text: Maturity is the work of experience alone; and therefore it requires time.
plain: Real understanding only comes from living it, and that can't be rushed.

text: The fatal tendency to be satisfied with words instead of trying to understand things--to learn phrases by heart, so that they may prove a refuge in time of need, exists, as a rule, even in children; and the tendency lasts on into manhood, making the knowledge of many learned persons to consist in mere verbiage.
plain: Knowing the phrases isn't knowing the thing. Words are a cheap stand-in for understanding.

text: Childhood and youth form the time for collecting materials, for getting a special and thorough knowledge of the individual and particular things.
plain: Youth is for gathering raw material. The big conclusions come later.

text: If you cut up a large diamond into little bits, it will entirely lose the value it had as a whole; and an army divided up into small bodies of soldiers, loses all its strength.
plain: Split your attention and you lose most of your power. Focus is the strength.

text: Noise is the most impertinent of all forms of interruption. It is not only an interruption, but also a disruption of thought.
plain: Interruptions don't just pause your thinking, they break it.

text: Hammering, the barking of dogs, and the crying of children are horrible to hear; but your only genuine assassin of thought is the crack of a whip; it exists for the purpose of destroying every pleasant moment of quiet thought that any one may now and then enjoy.
plain: One sudden loud crack can kill a good thought on the spot.

text: A man's body and the needs of his body are now everywhere treated with a tender indulgence. Is the thinking mind then, to be the only thing that is never to obtain the slightest measure of consideration or protection, to say nothing of respect?
plain: We guard the body carefully and treat the thinking mind as disposable. Guard yours.

text: There are some really beautifully landscapes in the world, but the human figures in them are poor, and you had not better look at them.
plain: Some things look better from far away.

text: The fly should be used as the symbol of impertinence and audacity; for whilst all other animals shun man more than anything else, and run away even before he comes near them, the fly lights upon his very nose.
plain: The pests have no fear of you. Boldness and being impressive are different things.

text: Wisdom which is only theoretical and never put into practice, is like a double rose; its color and perfume are delightful, but it withers away and leaves no seed.
plain: Wisdom you never use is just decoration. It dies without producing anything.

text: No rose without a thorn. Yes, but many a thorn without a rose.
plain: Pain doesn't guarantee reward. Plenty of hardship comes with no payoff.

text: As a child, as a youth, often even as a full-grown man, nay, his whole life long, he goes about among his fellows, looking like them and seemingly as unimportant. But let him alone; he will not die. Time will come and bring those who know how to value him.
plain: Anyone built to last looks ordinary for a long time. Time sorts it out.

text: The man who goes up in a balloon does not feel as though he were ascending; he only sees the earth sinking deeper under him.
plain: When you rise, you notice the ground falling away, not yourself climbing.

text: Your estimation of a man's size will be affected by the distance at which you stand from him, but in two entirely opposite ways according as it is his physical or his mental stature that you are considering. The one will seem smaller, the farther off you move; the other, greater.
plain: Distance shrinks people of body and magnifies people of mind.

text: Every hero is a Samson. The strong man succumbs to the intrigues of the weak and the many; and if in the end he loses all patience he crushes both them and himself.
plain: The strong get worn down by the many small ones, and sometimes break everything.

text: The moderate distance which they at last discover to be the only tolerable condition of intercourse, is the code of politeness and fine manners; and those who transgress it are roughly told--in the English phrase--to keep their distance.
plain: Closeness hurts, so politeness is just the right amount of space between people.

text: A man who has some heat in himself prefers to remain outside, where he will neither prick other people nor get pricked himself.
plain: If you're warm inside, you don't need to crowd others for warmth.

text: How shall a man be proud, when his conception is a crime, his birth a penalty, his life a labour, and death a necessity!
plain: Birth, work and death are not much to be proud of. Stay humble.

text: Do not consider his bad will, or his narrow understanding and perverse ideas; as the former may easily lead you to hate and the latter to despise him; but fix your attention only upon his sufferings, his needs, his anxieties, his pains.
plain: Look at what a person is suffering and it's hard to hate them.

text: The way to keep down hatred and contempt is certainly not to look for a man's alleged "dignity," but, on the contrary, to regard him as an object of pity.
plain: Don't judge people by their worth. See their pain and the hatred fades.

text: Envy builds the wall between Thee and Me thicker and stronger; Sympathy makes it slight and transparent; nay, sometimes it pulls down the wall altogether; and then the distinction between self and not-self vanishes.
plain: Envy makes you feel separate from people. Sympathy takes the wall down.

text: Courage, however, may also be explained as a readiness to meet ills that threaten at the moment, in order to avoid greater ills that lie in the future; whereas cowardice does the contrary.
plain: Courage is taking a smaller hit now to avoid a bigger one later.

text: Extravagance springs from a brutish limitation to the present moment, in comparison with which the future, existing as it does only in thought, is as nothing.
plain: The spender lives only in the present, and the future costs him nothing until it arrives.

text: Every human perfection is allied to a defect into which it threatens to pass; but it is also true that every defect is allied to a perfection.
plain: Every strength has a flaw next to it and every flaw a strength.

text: The cautious man seems to us a coward; the economical man, a miser; the spendthrift seems liberal; the rude fellow, downright and sincere; the foolhardy person looks as if he were going to work with a noble self-confidence; and so on in many other cases.
plain: We mistake flaws for virtues in people we've just met. Look closer.

text: Just as every man, though he be the greatest genius, has very definite limitations in some one sphere of knowledge, and thus attests his common origin with the essentially perverse and stupid mass of mankind, so also has every man something in his nature which is positively evil.
plain: Nobody is above flaws, not even the best. No need to hate yourself for yours.

text: A man who is unintelligent is very likely to show his perfidy, villainy and malice; whereas a clever man understands how to conceal these qualities.
plain: Fools show their malice openly, clever people hide it.

text: It is very necessary that a man should be apprised early in life that it is a masquerade in which he finds himself.
plain: Learn early that most people are wearing masks.

text: Man is at bottom a savage, horrible beast. We know it, if only in the business of taming and restraining him which we call civilisation.
plain: Civilization is a leash on something wild. Don't forget it's there.

text: In every man there dwells, first and foremost, a colossal egoism, which breaks the bounds of right and justice with the greatest freedom, as everyday life shows on a small scale, and as history on every page of it on a large.
plain: Everyone is deeply selfish and will bend rules for it. Plan around that.

text: That anger is not without its pleasure is a truth that was recorded even by Aristotle; and he quotes a passage from Homer, who declares anger to be sweeter than honey.
plain: Anger feels good, and that is exactly why it's dangerous.

text: No animal ever torments another for the mere purpose of tormenting, but man does it, and it is this that constitutes the diabolical feature in his character which is so much worse than the merely animal.
plain: Only people hurt others purely to hurt them.

text: Right in itself is powerless; in nature it is Might that rules.
plain: Being right is not enough. It needs strength behind it.

text: Formerly it was faith which was the chief support of the throne; nowadays it is credit.
plain: What holds power up changes with the age. Now it's trust in money.

text: Everywhere and at all times there has been much discontent with governments, laws and public regulations; for the most part, however, because men are always ready to make institutions responsible for the misery inseparable from human existence itself; which is, to speak mythically, the curse that was laid on Adam, and through him on the whole race.
plain: People blame governments for the pain that comes with being alive.
